narrative:
The model predicts you have a 30% chance of failing your final year, which is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses to strengthen your preparation.

The decision rests mainly on three key aspects of your situation. The most influential factor is that you have had no past class failures. While this might sound positive, students who ultimately pass almost always share this clean record; in your case the model sees it as insufficient to offset other risks. The second strongest influence is your strong desire to pursue higher education. This normally pushes predictions toward passing, but here it was not enough to overcome the overall pattern. The third important element is your low amount of free time after school. Most students who pass report having a medium or high level of free time, so your lower level worked against you.

Taken together, the lack of previous failures and your ambition to continue studying pulled the prediction slightly toward passing, but your limited free time after school pushed it more strongly toward failing. The combination resulted in the 30% risk that triggered the remedial requirement.

To improve, consider using some of your free time for structured study sessions each week. Even modest increases in focused academic effort, alongside your existing motivation for higher education, can meaningfully raise your chances of passing.
